$comment: Rules about how risk is characterised, measured, and made adverse enough to be worth modelling. Standards 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17. Five of the twelve are `manual-review` with `assurance: none` — the highest proportion outside rules/prohibited.json — and that concentration is not an accident. This is the part of the framework where the checkable property and the property that matters diverge most sharply: a label is visible in text, and whether a portfolio is actually diversified, whether an adverse case actually loses money, and whether an ordering is actually adverse are not.
$admissionTest: The five manual-review rules here were admitted under all five ADR 0005 questions rather than in spite of them: a reviewer can gather the evidence, evaluate it, explain the violation, and remediate it — by rewriting the scenario, reordering the series, or narrowing the claim. What was refused admission is named in each standard: Standard 13's softened correlation assumption, Standard 14's context-free defect framing, Standard 15's rounding-difference claim, Standard 16's objective-relative downside, Standard 17's recommended responses. Those stay in prose and are disclosed rather than absorbed to make the coverage number look better.

rules.title: A diversification claim names what it diversifies against and over what period it was measured
rules.description: A claim that holdings are diversified names the risk being diversified against, and where the claim rests on correlation, states the period over which that correlation was measured.
rules.rationale: "Diversified" with no object is a compliment rather than a claim, and a claim with no object cannot be falsified. Naming the risk makes it contestable; naming the measurement period exposes whether the correlation was estimated over a stretch that happened to be calm.
rules.remediation: State what the portfolio is diversified against — issuer, sector, geography, currency, factor — and give the period any correlation figure was measured over, with what happens to it under stress.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it establishes that a qualifier is PRESENT, never that it is RIGHT. "Diversified across sectors" attached to ten holdings in one sector passes this check, and no scan available to this repository sees the holdings. The substantive question is carried by risk.diversification-adequate, which claims no assurance at all.

rules.title: The portfolio is actually diversified against the risk claimed
rules.description: The holdings behave differently enough from one another, under the stress the claim concerns, to support the diversification the document asserts.
rules.rationale: This is the substance of Standard 13 and the only question about diversification that matters to a holder. A claim qualified perfectly and applied to ten holdings in one sector is a well-formed false statement, and the qualification makes it more persuasive rather than less.
rules.remediation: Examine the holdings, their issuers, sectors, currencies, and shared factor exposures, and record a judgement with evidence. Where the claim is not supported, narrow it to what the holdings actually deliver rather than restating it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person examines the holdings and records a judgement with evidence. There is no keyword list, no weight calculation, and no document scan that establishes how a set of holdings will behave under stress: the question needs the holdings themselves, their issuers and currencies, and a view about the future. A run reporting this rule as passing because it found the word "diversified" would be the framework committing the exact error it exists to catch.

rules.title: A document stating an allocation states a concentration measure
rules.description: Where an allocation is presented, a concentration measure — a sum-of-squared-weights index, or the share held by the largest positions — is presented with it.
rules.rationale: Concentration is the risk least visible to the person carrying it, and an allocation table does not display it: a reader sees rows, not the sum of squared weights. The measure has to be computed and stated, or it is simply not present for anyone.
rules.remediation: Compute a concentration measure from the allocation actually shown and state it beside the table, in a calc block so it can be recomputed.
rules.$assuranceNote: Structural and lexical. It establishes that a concentration figure is PRESENT, never that it is CORRECT or that it was computed from the allocation the document displays. A figure carried over from another portfolio passes, and whether the weights describe a real portfolio at all belongs to prohibited.fabricated-account-data, which is not automatable.

rules.title: A largest-holding figure is accompanied by a distribution measure
rules.description: Where the document states the size of its largest holding, it also states a measure describing how the remainder is distributed.
rules.rationale: A largest holding of 8% is consistent with twelve near-equal positions and with one position of 8% beside ninety trivial ones, and those portfolios carry different risks. The single figure conceals precisely the variation it appears to summarise.
rules.remediation: State a distribution measure beside the largest-holding figure — the concentration index, the top-five share, or the effective number of positions.
rules.$assuranceNote: Structural. It establishes that a second, distributional figure is PRESENT, never that it is CORRECT or that it describes the same allocation. Two figures that contradict each other both pass, because nothing here recomputes either from the weights on the page.

rules.title: Concentration is assessed across the whole financial position
rules.description: The concentration assessment covers the holder's position as a whole — employer equity, pension holdings, property, other accounts, and the income that pays for all of it — rather than one portfolio in isolation.
rules.rationale: The most dangerous concentration is the one that correlates with income. An employee whose salary, share awards, and pension all depend on one firm is concentrated in a way that no single-portfolio view shows, and the portfolio can look well spread while the position is not.
rules.remediation: Enumerate the exposures outside the portfolio under review — employer, property, other accounts, income source — and assess concentration against the total, marking whatever is unknown rather than assuming it away.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person records a judgement. The exposures this rule concerns are by definition outside the document being examined, so the checker cannot see the thing it would have to measure: a document analysing one account looks identical whether or not the other exposures were considered. It stays catalogued because a reviewer can gather that evidence, evaluate it, explain the violation, and remediate it.

rules.title: A stated volatility figure carries its period, sample, and estimator
rules.description: A standard deviation or other dispersion figure is stated with the periodicity it is measured at, the sample period it was estimated over, and how it was estimated.
rules.rationale: An annualised standard deviation estimated over a calm five years and one estimated across a crash are different numbers describing the same asset, and neither is comparable to a monthly figure. Without the qualifiers the number is not interpretable, only impressive.
rules.remediation: State the periodicity, the sample window, and the estimator beside the figure, and say whether the window contains a stress episode.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that qualifiers are PRESENT near the figure, never that they are ACCURATE or that the figure was computed as described. A monthly standard deviation labelled "annualised" passes, and so does a sample period stated as ten years for a figure estimated over three.

rules.title: Volatility is not presented as the whole of risk
rules.description: The document does not treat a dispersion statistic as a complete account of the risk taken, leaving permanent loss, illiquidity, counterparty failure, and the risk of missing the objective unaddressed.
rules.rationale: Volatility is measurable, which is why it stands in for risk, and it is silent about the failures that actually destroy plans: the holding that never recovers, the money that cannot be reached, the objective missed. A document that measures only what is measurable has narrowed the subject without announcing that it did.
rules.remediation: Name the risks the dispersion figure does not capture and address each, or state explicitly that the figure describes one dimension of risk and say which one.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person records a judgement. The compliant and the violating text differ by emphasis rather than by vocabulary — both discuss volatility, and one simply stops there — so no token's presence or absence separates them. A word list here would fail correct documents while missing the failure it was aimed at, and a rule people are right to ignore teaches them to ignore rules.

rules.title: A multi-period projection states a path measure beside its ending value
rules.description: A projection spanning multiple periods states a drawdown, worst-period, or other path measure alongside the ending value it reports.
rules.rationale: An end-point return does not determine the path, and the path is what a person lives through and abandons a plan during. Two series ending at the same value can differ by a 50% decline in the middle, and only one of them gets held to the end.
rules.remediation: State the maximum drawdown and the worst single period over the modelled path, computed in a calc block, beside the terminal figure.
rules.$assuranceNote: Structural: it establishes that a path figure is PRESENT beside the ending value, never that the figure is CORRECT or that the path modelled is a plausible one. A drawdown computed over a deliberately smooth path satisfies it completely.

rules.title: The adverse case models a decline, not a reduced gain
rules.description: The scenario labelled adverse describes an actual loss of value against the starting position, rather than a smaller gain than the base case.
rules.rationale: A scenario set whose worst member still gains is not a stress test; it is the base case shown four times. The substitution is easy to make and invisible in the table, because both forms are a percentage in a row labelled "adverse", and the adverse case is what determines whether a plan survives a bad decade.
rules.remediation: Set the adverse scenario to a genuine decline — an absolute loss, and over a long horizon a loss of purchasing power — and carry it through to what happens to the objective.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person reads the scenario and records a judgement. A scenario labelled "adverse" that models a 6% return instead of 8% is indistinguishable, to any scan, from one modelling a 30% fall: both are a label and a number in a table, and nothing in the document states what the number is relative to. It remains catalogued because a reviewer can see the figure, evaluate it, explain the violation, and remediate it by rewriting the scenario. Standard 19 R3 relies on this rule rather than adding a second id for the same question.

rules.title: A document with cash flows addresses the order of returns, not only their level
rules.description: Where a document contains withdrawal or contribution language, it addresses the effect of the order in which returns arrive, not only their average.
rules.rationale: With cash flows present, the same set of returns in a different order produces depletion in one direction and a large surplus in the other. An analysis that models only the average has modelled the single case where order does not matter, and then reported it as the answer.
rules.remediation: Model at least two orderings of the same returns, including one that front-loads the poor years, and state what each does to the objective.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical: it establishes that a discussion is PRESENT in a document that mentions cash flows, never that the discussion is ADEQUATE. A sentence reading "sequence risk was considered" satisfies it and demonstrates nothing. Where no policy declaration exists and the detector finds no withdrawal language the result is NOT_EVALUATED, not NOT_APPLICABLE — a detector that could grant itself an exemption would grant one to every document that failed to mention its withdrawals.

rules.title: A projection with no cash flows says that sequence risk does not apply
rules.description: Where a projection genuinely has no contributions or withdrawals, the document states that fact rather than omitting the subject.
rules.rationale: Omission and inapplicability look identical from outside the document. Saying that return order does not matter here, and why, is the only thing that distinguishes an analysis that considered sequence risk from one that never reached it.
rules.remediation: State that the projection has no cash flows and that return order therefore does not affect the outcome, or declare the rule not-applicable in policy with a reason and a revisit condition.
rules.$assuranceNote: Lexical. It establishes that a statement of inapplicability is PRESENT, never that the statement is TRUE: a document with withdrawals that asserts it has none passes. The tooling deliberately refuses to infer inapplicability from the absence of cash-flow language, because that inference would exempt precisely the documents that failed to mention their withdrawals.

rules.title: The adverse ordering places the poor returns early
rules.description: The series presented as the adverse ordering actually places the worst returns at the start of the withdrawal period, where they do the most damage.
rules.rationale: An adverse ordering that puts the bad years late is arithmetically a different and far gentler claim. The whole of sequence risk is that early losses compound against a balance that withdrawals are already shrinking, and an ordering that misses that models nothing.
rules.remediation: Reorder the modelled series so the poor returns fall in the first years of withdrawals, and show the resulting path beside the favourable ordering.
rules.$assuranceNote: Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person examines the modelled path and records a judgement. Documents typically present an outcome rather than the series that produced it, and where the series is shown, whether its ordering is genuinely adverse for these particular cash flows is an arithmetic question about a path the checker was never given. A reviewer can see the ordering, evaluate it, and remediate it by reordering the series.
